what_it_does: Division is one of the harder arithmetic operations to build in hardware: standard binary circuits need multiple clock cycles and complicated control logic to produce a quotient. The difficulty compounds when trying to perform division inside a memory chip rather than in a separate processor, because memory substrates are noisy and prone to manufacturing variation that flips bits unpredictably. This paper uses stochastic computing (SC) — a technique that represents numbers not as a fixed binary pattern but as a random stream of 0s and 1s whose proportion (e.g., 75 ones in 100 bits) encodes the value 0.75. Division then reduces to an extremely simple logic operation on two such bit-streams, and the approach is naturally tolerant of occasional bit errors. The physical substrate is a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) — a nanoscale device that stores a bit as the magnetic orientation of a thin layer and can switch states with a small current — which is used to generate and store the stochastic bit-streams for logic-in-memory operation.
